content:
Bloomberg published a report yesterday stating that Apple is about to launch a brand-new "Apple Upgrade" leasing contract to replace the existing iPhone Upgrade Program.

There appear to be two major differences between the two, one of which may be quite worrying…

The iPhone Upgrade Program operates in a straightforward manner. The purchase price is spread over 24 monthly installments, and once the two-year period ends, the device is entirely yours. There are no credit charges during the period.

(Additionally, you may also choose to upgrade to a new iPhone after 12 months. At that point, a new two-year contract will commence, and you effectively sell the old device back to Apple using the payments you have already made.)

Apple has yet to make any official announcement regarding the replacement programme, so we cannot confirm exactly how it will operate. However, according to Bloomberg, the new programme will cover most other Apple products, with Mac products having a three-year lease term. So far, everything seems fairly reasonable.

However, what is concerning is that the report suggests the new programme will operate in much the same way as an automobile lease. Under such contracts, you do not pay the full purchase price of the product, but rather only the depreciation amount of the product during the lease term, plus any interest. Once the lease expires, you do not own the product—you are essentially merely renting it.

Similarly, assuming it works the same way as an auto lease, at the end of the lease term you must return the product, or pay a "residual settlement," which is the difference between the depreciation amount and the full price of the product.

Of course, this means the monthly payment will be lower than under the current programme. Some might consider this a good thing, as it makes Apple products more affordable for more people.

However, what is worth noting is that most people will not save extra money each month to pay this residual sum when the lease ends. The most common scenario with auto leases is that people return the car at the end of the lease, then sign a new lease for a new car. They are essentially trapped in a never-ending cycle, never truly owning the product.

If the new Apple Upgrade programme operates in the same way, the situation would be identical. Those who purchase in this manner will not only be able to keep their existing phone for many years, but will also be forced to upgrade their iPhone every two years, or their Mac every three years. Even without any interest expenses, in the long run, the total cost of ownership would increase significantly.

Furthermore, if the report is accurate and AppleCare+ is not included, users could find themselves in situations where the device is lost, stolen, or severely damaged beyond repair during the lease term. Not only would they still need to continue making monthly payments for a device they no longer have, but they would also have to pay the residual settlement when the lease expires.

I understand that Apple wishes to streamline operations with a single upgrade programme, hence the withdrawal of the existing one. However, I believe a better approach for consumers would be to offer programme options that allow everyone to enjoy credit arrangements while deciding their own upgrade pace.

What are your thoughts on this? Feel free to share your views in the comments section.
